nodes.name: Peter
nodes.role: Apostle; Irenaeus says he and Paul founded the Church at Rome.

nodes.name: Paul
nodes.role: Apostle to the Gentiles; wrote letters to Timothy and Titus.

nodes.name: John
nodes.role: Apostle and evangelist; the early writers place his later years at Ephesus.

nodes.name: Mark
nodes.role: Called Peter's "son" in 1 Peter; later writers call him Peter's interpreter.

nodes.name: Timothy
nodes.role: Paul's younger co-worker; recipient of two letters.

nodes.name: Titus
nodes.role: Paul's co-worker, left in Crete.

nodes.name: Linus
nodes.role: Named by Irenaeus as the first bishop of Rome after the apostles.

nodes.name: Anacletus
nodes.role: Second in Irenaeus's list of the bishops of Rome.

nodes.name: Clement of Rome
nodes.role: Bishop of Rome; wrote to the Corinthians about discord.

words.quote: Our apostles also knew, through our Lord Jesus Christ
words.note: Chapter 44 of his letter, on the apostles providing for orderly ministry. The bundled text of this chapter is cut short at its footnote marks, so we quote only the words that survive.

words.quote: there would be strife on account of the office
words.note: The same chapter, a later stretch of the same sentence in the bundled text.

nodes.name: Ignatius of Antioch
nodes.role: Bishop of Antioch; wrote seven letters on the road to martyrdom at Rome.

nodes.name: Polycarp of Smyrna
nodes.role: Bishop of Smyrna; his letter and the account of his martyrdom survive.

words.quote: But the most admirable Polycarp, when he first heard [that he was sought for], was in no measure disturbed
words.note: From the church of Smyrna's account of his martyrdom.

nodes.name: Papias of Hierapolis
nodes.role: Bishop who collected sayings of the Lord from those who had known the apostles. Only fragments survive.

nodes.name: John the Presbyter
nodes.role: An "elder John" whom Papias says he heard. Eusebius thought him a different man from the apostle.

nodes.name: Justin Martyr
nodes.role: Philosopher and apologist; martyred at Rome.

nodes.name: Tatian
nodes.role: Hearer of Justin; later left the Church.

nodes.name: Rhodo
nodes.role: Writer against the heretics; listed by Jerome as a disciple of Tatian.

nodes.name: Irenaeus of Lyons
nodes.role: Bishop of Lyons; wrote Against Heresies and appealed to the succession of bishops.

nodes.name: Hippolytus of Rome
nodes.role: Roman presbyter and writer, whom later editors call Irenaeus's pupil.

nodes.name: Pantaenus
nodes.role: First known head of the catechetical school at Alexandria.

nodes.name: Clement of Alexandria
nodes.role: Teacher at Alexandria; wrote the Instructor and Stromata.

words.quote: Well, they preserving the tradition of the blessed doctrine derived directly from the holy apostles, Peter, James, John, and Paul
words.note: Clement describes his own teachers in this way. He does not name them in this sentence; an editor's note in our text suggests the last of them was Pantaenus.

nodes.name: Origen
nodes.role: Teacher and biblical scholar at Alexandria and Caesarea.

nodes.name: Heraclas
nodes.role: Origen's assistant, later bishop of Alexandria.

nodes.name: Gregory Thaumaturgus
nodes.role: Pupil of Origen; bishop of Neo-Caesarea in Pontus.

nodes.name: Pamphilus of Caesarea
nodes.role: Presbyter and martyr; friend of Eusebius.

nodes.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
nodes.role: Bishop and historian; wrote the Church History.

nodes.name: Tertullian
nodes.role: Carthaginian writer, the first great Latin Father.

nodes.name: Caecilius
nodes.role: Carthaginian presbyter who led Cyprian to the faith.

nodes.name: Cyprian of Carthage
nodes.role: Bishop of Carthage and martyr.

nodes.name: Pontius the Deacon
nodes.role: Cyprian's deacon, who wrote his Life.

nodes.name: Cornelius of Rome
nodes.role: Bishop of Rome; Cyprian wrote to him about Novatian.

nodes.name: Alexander of Alexandria
nodes.role: Bishop of Alexandria at the time of Arius.

nodes.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
nodes.role: Bishop of Alexandria; defender of Nicaea; author of the Life of Antony.

nodes.name: Antony of Egypt
nodes.role: Desert monk whose Life shaped early monasticism.

nodes.name: Basil the Great
nodes.role: Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia.

nodes.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
nodes.role: Friend of Basil; bishop and theologian.

nodes.name: Gregory of Nyssa
nodes.role: Basil's younger brother; bishop of Nyssa.

nodes.name: Jerome
nodes.role: Scholar who translated the Latin Bible.

nodes.name: Simplicianus
nodes.role: Elder priest at Milan, later bishop; counselled Augustine.

nodes.name: Ambrose of Milan
nodes.role: Bishop of Milan.

nodes.name: Augustine of Hippo
nodes.role: Bishop of Hippo; wrote the Confessions.

nodes.name: Valerius of Hippo
nodes.role: Bishop of Hippo who ordained Augustine presbyter.

nodes.name: Possidius of Calama
nodes.role: Bishop of Calama, friend of Augustine and author of his Life.

nodes.name: Alypius of Thagaste
nodes.role: Augustine's friend from boyhood; later a bishop.

edges.quote: to Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace
edges.note: Paul addresses Timothy as his child in the faith. Scripture states this, not a later tradition.

edges.quote: The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.
edges.note: Paul asks Timothy to hand on what he heard. This is the clearest line in Scripture about passing teaching on.

edges.quote: to Titus, my true child according to a common faith
edges.note: Paul writes to Titus and later tells him to appoint elders in every city.

edges.quote: So does Mark, my son.
edges.note: Peter calls Mark his son. Later writers add that Mark was his interpreter.

edges.quote: committed into the hands of Linus the office of the episcopate
edges.note: Irenaeus says the Church at Rome was founded by Peter and Paul, and that the apostles then gave the office to Linus. These are his words, not our claim.

edges.quote: founded and organized at Rome by the two most glorious apostles, Peter and Paul
edges.note: The same passage names Paul together with Peter as founders of the Roman Church. Irenaeus adds that Paul mentions Linus in the letters to Timothy.

edges.quote: To him succeeded Anacletus
edges.note: Irenaeus lists the bishops of Rome in order. Early lists differ in the order of the first names.

edges.quote: in the third place from the apostles, Clement was allotted the bishopric
edges.note: Irenaeus puts Clement third from the apostles.

edges.quote: as he had seen the blessed apostles, and had been conversant with them
edges.note: Irenaeus says "the apostles", and does not name Peter alone. We join Peter and Paul to Clement because Irenaeus named them as the founders at Rome.

edges.quote: as he had seen the blessed apostles, and had been conversant with them
edges.note: Same sentence as the edge from Peter. See that note.

edges.quote: Take up the epistle of the blessed Apostle Paul.
edges.note: Clement points the Corinthians back to Paul's letter to them.

edges.quote: the accounts which he gave of his intercourse with John and with the others who had seen the Lord
edges.note: Irenaeus, in a letter quoted by Eusebius, recalls Polycarp telling of his time with John.

edges.quote: by apostles in Asia, appointed bishop of the Church in Smyrna
edges.note: Irenaeus says apostles in Asia appointed Polycarp. He says "apostles", not John by name.

edges.quote: I am able to describe the very place in which the blessed Polycarp sat as he discoursed
edges.note: Irenaeus, writing to Florinus, remembers hearing Polycarp as a boy.

edges.quote: whom I also saw in my early youth
edges.note: In Against Heresies 3.3.4 Irenaeus says he saw Polycarp when he was young.

edges.quote: Papias, an ancient man, who was a hearer of John, and a friend of Polycarp
edges.note: This is what Irenaeus says, as quoted by Eusebius. Eusebius then doubts that Papias heard an apostle. See the next edge.

edges.quote: makes it manifest that he was not himself a hearer and eye-witness of the holy apostles
edges.note: Eusebius, in the same passage, reads Papias's own preface differently. So the link between Papias and the apostle John is disputed in our sources.

edges.quote: he heard in person Aristion and the presbyter John
edges.note: Eusebius reports that Papias heard "the presbyter John". Eusebius took this to be a second John.

edges.quote: received the sayings of the apostles from those who accompanied them
edges.note: Eusebius's own summary of Papias's preface.

edges.quote: Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus, to Polycarp, Bishop of the Church of the Smyrnæans
edges.note: Ignatius's letter to Polycarp. It shows the two men knew each other; it does not say who taught whom.

edges.quote: not only in the case of the blessed Ignatius, and Zosimus, and Rufus
edges.note: Polycarp's letter to the Philippians holds up Ignatius as an example of patience.

edges.quote: He was a hearer of Justin's
edges.note: Irenaeus says Tatian heard Justin, and that he fell away after Justin's martyrdom.

edges.quote: Rhodo, the disciple of Tatian
edges.note: Jerome's list of writers gives this heading. Only the list survives in our bundle of the Lives, not the full entry.

edges.quote: He is the disciple of Irenæus
edges.note: This is the editor's opening note in our volume of Hippolytus. It is a later scholar's statement, not Hippolytus's own words.

edges.quote: he was the teacher of Clement
edges.note: The translator's note on Eusebius says this about Pantaenus. Clement himself names no teacher in the passage we have.

edges.quote: since Origen was one of his pupils he can hardly have left long before that time
edges.note: A note by the translator of Eusebius. Eusebius himself says Origen taught in the school at Alexandria.

edges.quote: he selected Heraclas, who was a zealous student of divine things … made him his associate in the work of instruction
edges.note: Eusebius says Origen chose Heraclas from his pupils to share the teaching.

edges.quote: many pupils came to him not only from the vicinity, but also from other countries. Among these Theodorus, the same that was distinguished among the bishops of our day under the name of Gregory
edges.note: Eusebius names Gregory (called Theodorus) among Origen's pupils.

edges.quote: after many years’ instruction under that teacher
edges.note: The heading to Gregory's farewell oration to Origen, in the translators' volume.

edges.quote: Gregory of Nyssa about a century later wrote a life of Gregory Thaumaturgus
edges.note: The translator's note. This is a second link: Nyssa wrote about the earlier Gregory.

edges.quote: a Life of Pamphilus the Martyr, from whom on account of friendship he took his surname, in three books
edges.note: From the old testimonies gathered in our volume of Eusebius.

edges.quote: Six Apologies in Behalf of Origen
edges.note: The same testimony lists his defence of Origen.

edges.quote: the elaborate Defense of Origen, composed by Pamphilus and himself
edges.note: The translator's introduction to Eusebius says Pamphilus and Eusebius wrote the Defense together.

edges.quote: Cyprian is the spiritual son and pupil of Tertullian
edges.note: The editor's introduction says this. Our bundled texts do not give Cyprian's own words about it.

edges.quote: who had converted him from his worldly errors to the acknowledgment of the true divinity
edges.note: Pontius says the presbyter Caecilius brought Cyprian to the faith.

edges.quote: The Life and Passion of Cyprian, Bishop and Martyr. By Pontius the Deacon.
edges.note: Pontius was Cyprian's deacon and wrote his Life.

edges.quote: To Cornelius, on His Refusal to Receive Novatian
edges.note: One of Cyprian's letters to the bishop of Rome.

edges.quote: Athanasius succeeded him at the end of the same year
edges.note: The editor's note to Socrates. The original sentence is not in our bundled text.

edges.quote: Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria, hath lately set forth in a several volume, intituled of his life, his manners and converasiton
edges.note: Socrates, in an old English translation quoted in our volume, says Athanasius wrote Antony's Life.

edges.quote: But when he was departing, and we were setting him forth on his way
edges.note: Inside the Life, the narrator says "we" saw Antony off. An editor's note takes the narrator to be Athanasius.

edges.quote: a conversation arose (suggested by his account) on Antony the Egyptian monk
edges.note: Augustine tells how a friend's story of Antony, and a copy of his Life, moved them before his conversion.

edges.quote: For it brought me to know Basil more perfectly
edges.note: Gregory's funeral oration says Athens is where he came to know Basil.

edges.quote: To Basil His Comrade
edges.note: The heading of Gregory's first letter to Basil.

edges.quote: that man of God, that mouth of piety, Basil
edges.note: Gregory of Nyssa speaks of Basil in Against Eunomius.

edges.quote: My teacher, Gregory of Nazianzus, when I once asked him to explain Luke
edges.note: Jerome calls Gregory his teacher in Letter 52.

edges.quote: To Jerome, His Most Beloved Lord, and Brother and Fellow-Presbyter
edges.note: Augustine's first letter to Jerome.

edges.quote: the father of Ambrose (a Bishop now) in receiving Thy grace
edges.note: Augustine says Simplicianus was like a father to Ambrose in the faith.

edges.quote: when that man of Thine, Simplicianus, related to me this of Victorinus, I was on fire to imitate him
edges.note: Augustine went to Simplicianus for counsel and heard him tell of Victorinus.

edges.quote: To him was I unknowing led by Thee, that by him I might knowingly be led to Thee. That man of God received me as a father
edges.note: Augustine's own words about meeting Ambrose at Milan.

edges.quote: To My Lord Bishop Valerius, Most Blessed and Venerable, My Father Most Warmly Cherished
edges.note: Augustine, then a presbyter, writes to the bishop who ordained him.

edges.quote: Possidius, in his Life of Augustin, ch. 18, says
edges.note: A translator's note in our Augustine volume cites Possidius's Life of Augustine. The Life itself is not in the library.

edges.quote: chiefly and most familiarly did I speak thereof with Alypius and Nebridius
edges.note: Augustine names Alypius as a close friend in the Confessions.

traditional.note: Later writers say Ignatius followed Peter (or Evodius) as bishop of Antioch. No text in our library states it plainly, so we draw no quote.
An editor in our Polycarp volume guesses Ignatius and Polycarp were fellow pupils of John. This is a conjecture, not a source statement.
Later writers link Mark, Peter and Papias through a saying about Mark as Peter's interpreter. That saying is not intact in our bundled text, so we draw no quote.
